extracted.intended_audience: cozy mystery writers and readers (authors, fans, and commentators of Golden Age detective fiction)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and commentary on Knox's 'Ten Commandments'—a set of fair-play rules for writing Golden Age / cozy detective fiction, with notes on which rules still apply and how to adapt them for modern cozies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 1 — The criminal must be someone mentioned in the early part of the story, but must not be anyone whose thoughts the reader has been allowed to follow
rubrics_metrics.description: “The criminal must be someone mentioned in the early part of the story, but must not be anyone whose thoughts the reader has been allowed to follow.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is sometimes broken (e.g., Agatha Christie uses it effectively), but it's difficult to pull off without feeling unfair; not generally recommended for less-experienced authors. Implies that suspect must be introduced early so the reader has a fair chance, and the author should not give the reader access to the criminal's inner thoughts if the criminal is to remain a mystery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 2 — All supernatural or preternatural agencies are ruled out as a matter of course
rubrics_metrics.description: “All supernatural or preternatural agencies are ruled out as a matter of course.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally forbids supernatural explanations. The blog notes modern cozies often include paranormal hooks (witchcraft, mild psychic powers), which can be allowed so long as the crime isn't simply solved by magic (avoid 'the detective casts a spell and now knows who committed the crime'). Paranormal detectives may justify some exceptions, but outright deus-ex-machina magical solutions remain poor fair-play practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 4 — No hitherto undiscovered poisons or appliances needing long scientific explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: “No hitherto undiscovered poisons may be used, nor any appliance which will need a long scientific explanation at the end.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knox means the poison should be known to medical science and, if possible, detectable by autopsy. This is recommended: if authorities examine the body, the cause of death should not be inconclusive. Poisons that disguise a murder to casual observation are acceptable so long as the eventual cause of death can be determined. Also forbids plot devices that require long, implausible scientific exposition to resolve—these risk cheating the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 6 — No accident must ever help the detective, nor must he ever have an unaccountable intuition which proves to be right
rubrics_metrics.description: “No accident must ever help the detective, nor must he ever have an unaccountable intuition which proves to be right.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knox clarifies that reasonable flashes of insight grounded in previously observed evidence are allowed; the prohibition targets unaccountable instincts that suddenly point the detective to a solution without prior groundwork (e.g., searching the grandfather clock because of an unaccountable instinct). The detective should discover things through work and deduction (or by thorough searching). Exceptions are more tolerable if the detective is associated with the paranormal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 7 — The detective must not himself commit the crime
rubrics_metrics.description: “The detective must not himself commit the crime.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered an important rule: it's unfair for a detective-character (vouched-for by the author) to secretly be the criminal and then gather suspects to reveal it. A criminal posing as an inspector or detective is acceptable if the story provides reason to doubt their identity earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 8 — The detective must not light on any clues which are not instantly produced for the inspection of the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: “The detective must not light on any clues which are not instantly produced for the inspection of the reader.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author should not withhold crucial evidence from the reader; if the crucial piece of evidence isn't visible or producible to the audience, it feels like cheating and the mystery is unsolvable for the reader. This enforces 'fair play'—all necessary clues that lead to the solution should be available to readers when the detective finds them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 9 — The Watson/stupid friend must not conceal any thoughts and should be slightly below average intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: “The stupid friend of the detective, the Watson, must not conceal any thoughts which pass through his mind; his intelligence must be slightly, but very slightly, below that of the average reader.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies only when there is a 'Watson' character. The assistant should not hide inner thoughts (which would deprive the reader of information) and should be only marginally less intelligent than the average reader—making them too stupid is a trap. It's difficult to write but aiming for a lightly less-capable foil keeps fairness and interest. Commenters note the danger of 'TSTL' (Too Stupid To Live) characters who behave implausibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 5 — No Chinaman must figure in the story (historical racist trope)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Rule 5 — ‘No Chinaman must figure in the story.’”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule reflects a historical attempt to ban lazy, racist stereotyping—specifically the trope of using an inscrutable Chinese character as a go-to villain. Modern interpretation: avoid ethnic stereotyping and using marginalized groups as lazy villain shorthand. The page's comments note the rule's racist phrasing and explain the intent: to prohibit a tired, prejudiced trope; in modern terms, the spirit is 'do not rely on stereotyped ethnic villains.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggested rule — The sleuth should not be put in peril in every book of a series
rubrics_metrics.description: Author's suggested substitution/rule: avoid making the sleuth fall into peril in each book/episode as a routine plot device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blogger dislikes recurring 'peril-as-spectacle' that makes sleuths seem stupid/unlucky; repeatedly endangering the protagonist can feel contrived and dumb the character down. Aim for realism in consequences and avoid 'idiot plots' where characters repeatedly make implausibly bad choices to keep danger alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair-play principle (overarching desideratum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of Knox's Commandments embody a 'fair play' expectation: readers should be given a fair chance to solve the mystery because necessary clues and information are made available in a non-deceptive way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple rules enforce fairness: suspects introduced early, no hidden clues, no deus ex machina (magic or undiscovered poisons/appliances), detective's insights should be justifiable. Anti-patterns include late-only revelations, evidence revealed only to the detective, unexamined miraculous scientific devices, and solutions by pure chance. The blogger emphasizes that many of Knox's rules still hold up for creating a satisfying, solvable cozy mystery.
